_scope_definitions.all: Every survey experiment in the corpus.
_scope_definitions.list_experiment: The paper states it uses a list experiment / item-count technique — respondents in a treatment group receive a list containing a sensitive item and report only a count. Fires on the paper's own naming of a list/item-count/unmatched-count design. Does NOT fire on a direct sensitive question, a randomized-response design, or an endorsement design.
_scope_definitions.nonrandomized_moderator: The paper states it estimates or interprets the effect of a variable it did NOT randomly assign — a measured respondent characteristic, attitude, exposure, or covariate used as an explanatory, moderating, or mediating variable in a causal claim. Fires when the paper reads a non-randomized variable's association as its effect. Does NOT fire on effects of the randomized treatment itself, nor on associations the paper explicitly labels non-causal.
_scope_definitions.conjoint: The paper states it uses a conjoint / fully-randomized attribute design in which respondents evaluate profiles whose attributes are independently randomized. Fires on the paper's own naming of a conjoint or randomized-attribute profile design. Does NOT fire on a single-vignette design that manipulates one or two features, nor on a list/endorsement design.
_scope_definitions.factor_isolation_claim: The paper states its manipulation isolates the effect of one specific factor, attributing the treatment-control difference to that single factor. A design presented only as estimating the combined effect of a bundled treatment, with no claim to isolate one factor, does NOT fire it.
_scope_definitions.endorsement_experiment: The paper states it uses an endorsement experiment — respondents rate policies, and a randomly assigned subset sees the policy endorsed by an actor. Fires on the paper's own naming of an endorsement design. Does NOT fire on a list experiment or a direct actor-approval question.
_scope_definitions.belief_effect: The paper states its estimand is the effect of a belief or of respondents' understanding of a manipulated attribute (an epistemic effect) — it interprets its manipulation as changing what respondents believe about a focal factor. Fires on the paper's own framing of the quantity of interest as a belief/attribute effect. Does NOT fire on a design that interprets its manipulation only as the effect of the message/wording itself, with no belief-level claim.
_scope_definitions.mediation: The paper states it performs a mediation analysis or decomposes an effect through a mediator that it measured rather than randomized. Fires on the paper's own naming of a mediator / indirect effect with an observed mediator. Does NOT fire on a design that randomizes the mediator in a factorial arm, nor on a paper with no mediation claim.
_scope_definitions.subgroup_or_conditioning: The paper states it estimates a subgroup, conditional, or moderated effect, or conditions/subsets its estimate on a respondent-measured variable. Fires when the paper reports heterogeneous effects by a respondent variable, interacts treatment with a covariate, or conditions on a post-treatment quantity. Does NOT fire on a paper reporting only a single overall treatment effect with no conditioning.
_scope_definitions.direct_list_comparison: The paper states it reads the gap between a direct-question estimate and a list-experiment (or other indirect) estimate as a measure of sensitivity or social-desirability bias. A list experiment alone, a direct question alone, or using both only to triangulate a prevalence without interpreting their difference as bias, does NOT fire it.
_scope_definitions.survey_weights: The paper states it applies survey/selection/sampling weights in estimating a population-level (PATE) effect. Reporting demographics or design features without using weights in estimation does NOT fire it.
_scope_definitions.list_regression: The paper states it estimates a regression model (linear least squares, nonlinear least squares, or maximum likelihood) relating respondent covariates to list-experiment responses. Fires when the paper names such a multivariate list-experiment estimator. Does NOT fire on a paper reporting only a difference-in-means prevalence or unadjusted subgroup means.
_scope_definitions.list_predictor: The paper states it uses a list-experiment quantity (a predicted/fitted sensitive-item value or estimated proportion) as an explanatory variable in a further outcome model — a two-step or multi-stage procedure. Fires on the paper's own description of feeding a list-experiment estimate into a downstream regression. Does NOT fire on a one-stage list-experiment analysis that reports prevalence or covariate associations directly.
_scope_definitions.repeated_tasks: The paper states each respondent contributes more than one observation to the analysis — multiple conjoint tasks, repeated rating/choice tasks, repeated vignettes, or multiple items analyzed jointly per respondent. Fires on the paper's own description of a within-respondent repeated-measures structure. Does NOT fire on a between-subjects design where each respondent contributes a single observation.
_scope_definitions.population_inference: The paper states it generalizes its treatment-effect estimate to a real-world or target population — it describes its estimand as a population effect, claims representativeness, or applies survey weights to a population. Fires on the paper's own generalization/representativeness language. Does NOT fire on a paper that explicitly confines its claims to the study sample or presents itself as an internal-validity demonstration.
_scope_definitions.framing_treatment: The paper states it compares two or more substantive framing/wording/message arms to estimate a treatment effect on attitudes. Fires when the design contrasts message or frame conditions. Does NOT fire on list/conjoint/endorsement measurement designs where a control list or reference category is intrinsic to the method.

evidence.quote: Like any two-step estimator, the calculation of valid standard errors must take into account the estimation uncertainty from both the first and second steps.

claim: Generalizing an experimental estimate to a target population is warranted only on a stated basis — a probability sample with appropriate weights, or an explicit assumption (representativeness / homogeneous effects). A convenience sample's relation to the population is generally unknowable, and demographic matching or reweighting does not establish it.
observable: Whether the paper that generalizes to a population states the basis for the generalization (probability sampling + weights, or an explicit assumption), rather than generalizing from a convenience/non-probability sample without justification.
pass_condition: The paper states the basis for its population claim — a probability sample with appropriate weighting, or an explicit representativeness / effect-homogeneity assumption it argues for.
flag_condition: The paper generalizes its estimate to a population from a convenience or non-probability sample without stating a supporting assumption or design basis.
severity_basis: Sources state a convenience sample's relation to the population is unknowable and that population claims require justified design/analysis choices.
requirement_statement: A paper generalizing to a population must state its sampling/weighting basis or an explicit generalization assumption.

evidence.quote: when one uses a convenience sample, its relationship to the population of interest is unknown and typically unknowable. Thus, one cannot assuredly conclude it generalizes, even if the demographics of the sample seem to match the demographics of the larger population of interest (e.g. U.S. citizens) or if data are reweighted to match population distributions.

it is increasingly difficult to claim purely design-based population inferences from any sample. Such challenges highlight the need in all survey-based research of thinking through and justifying design and analytic decisions if the inferential goal is to make claims about a given population as a whole.

Due to probability sampling of participants from the U.S. population, the experimental effects drawn from the weighted TESS sample should provide unbiased estimates of treatment effects for the U.S. adult population as a whole.

the presence of such ceiling and floor effects would lead to the underestimation of the population proportion of those who would answer affirmatively for the sensitive item.

claim: A framing/wording experiment that compares only treatment arms without a no-treatment control yields an ambiguous contrast — a difference between arms cannot reveal which frame moved attitudes; omitting the control obliges the authors to qualify their conclusions.
observable: Whether the design includes a no-treatment control/baseline condition, or, if it is deliberately omitted, whether the paper qualifies its conclusions.
pass_condition: The paper includes a no-treatment control/baseline arm, or, where one is deliberately omitted, qualifies its conclusions accordingly.
flag_condition: The paper compares treatment/framing arms with no control baseline and does not qualify its conclusions.
severity_basis: The source states arm-only comparisons are ambiguous and deliberate omission of a control obliges qualification.
requirement_statement: A framing/wording experiment must include a control baseline or qualify conclusions when one is omitted.

evidence.quote: Surprisingly many studies lack control groups, rendering their results ambiguous.
With no baseline, the researcher confronted with a significant difference between responses across treatments cannot know whether one frame or the other (or both) shapes attitudes.
When researchers choose deliberately to omit a control, they must qualify their findings appropriately.
